content: Facility-level staff involved in HIV surveillance and patient monitoring include clinic managers, healthcare providers, data officers or clerks, records assistants, pharmacy managers (or pharmacy technicians if no manager is available), and laboratory managers (or laboratory technicians if no manager is available). General Information for Interviews with Key Informants: 1. Begin by greeting the key informant. 2. If you have not previously met the informant, introduce yourself. 3. Express gratitude to the informant for taking the time to discuss HIV surveillance. 4. Provide a brief overview of the purpose of the situational assessment. 5. Assure the informant that all responses will remain confidential and will only be used to inform planning activities. Inform them that they are not obligated to answer any questions they are uncomfortable with and can end the interview at any time. Situational Assessment for Case Surveillance: HIV Notification Process: 1. Policies and Regulations: What are the national and subnational policies, laws, or regulations governing HIV disease notification? Who is required to report, and which entities are involved? 2. Reporting Pathway: What is the process for reporting HIV data? How frequently is data reported? 3. Data Aggregation: Are data reported in disaggregated or aggregated formats? If aggregated, at what level does aggregation occur? 4. Reportable Events: What events are reportable (e.g., HIV diagnosis, sentinel events)? 5. Reported Variables: What variables are included in reports? Are personal identifiers (e.g., sex, date of birth, full or partial name) included? 6. Key Populations: Are data on key populations (e.g., commercial sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs) included? If so, how are they incorporated? 7. Confidentiality and Security: How are confidentiality and data security addressed at diagnosis, during treatment, and in ongoing care? 8. Data Analysis: Is there a dedicated person or team for data analysis at the national, subnational, or facility level? How are analysis results presented, and is there a standard report format? Who receives these results? 9. Data Management: How much time is spent on data entry, editing, and storage? Has the country invested in macro databases for patient monitoring and case surveillance? At what levels? 10. De-duplication: Is there a process for de-duplicating records? How are duplication issues communicated back to health facilities? 11. Integration with Patient Monitoring: How is case surveillance linked to patient monitoring? Has the surveillance system been evaluated, and if so, what were the findings? 12. Outcome Analysis: Is there a link between age and retention, elimination of mother-to-child transmission, service quality, or other outcomes? Specify. 13. Data Utilization: How are patient monitoring and case surveillance data used at national, subnational, and facility levels? What are the plans for transitioning to electronic-based reporting, and at what levels? 14. Feedback Systems: Are there standard dashboards and feedback routines (electronic or paper-based)? How are these data routinely used for program decisions at various levels? Data Needs for HIV Surveillance and Reporting: 1. What data are used for HIV strategic planning? What data are currently used to measure HIV prevalence and the care cascade (e.g., number diagnosed, in care, on ART, virally suppressed)? 2. How could case-based reporting assist in surveillance activities? Leadership for HIV Surveillance and Reporting: 1. Is there a designated person responsible for HIV notification? 2. Is there leadership support or investment in case surveillance? Who are the appropriate leaders to engage? 3. Is there a technical working group for HIV or disease surveillance? 4. Is there a national strategy for collecting and using HIV data? Does it include case surveillance? Human Resources for HIV Surveillance: 1. National Level: What surveillance staff report to the HIV SI director or infectious disease notification director (e.g., surveillance coordinator, data manager, epidemiologist)? 2. Subnational Level: Are there HIV program managers or surveillance directors? Is there a data manager responsible for data quality checks, and at what levels? 3. Facility Level: Are there on-site personnel who systematically report cases, or is additional surveillance staff required? Who is responsible for data quality checks? What training is required for data collection, cleaning, and interpretation? Other Case-Based Notifiable Diseases: 1. Is case-based notification used for other diseases? If so, how does it work, and what is its performance? What diseases are reported on a case basis, and why? 2. Does notification include patient names? What is the reporting process (e.g., by whom, frequency, format, variables, data use)? 3. Has the surveillance system been evaluated? If so, what were the findings? HIV Diagnosis and Testing: 1. Where are HIV tests conducted (e.g., healthcare facilities providing HIV care, non-HIV care facilities, home-based or self-testing, surveys)? 2. Are tests conducted outside facilities recorded? If so, how? 3. Following a positive test, are individuals referred to care and tracked to ensure they access HIV care/treatment facilities? If yes, what is the referral and tracking process, and what information is collected? Clinical Care: 1. At enrollment into care and initiation of ART, are CD4 and VL tests conducted? Are these routine for monitoring or only done to confirm the need for medication changes? 2. Are there plans to expand VL testing? If so, what are the plans and timeline? Where is VL testing conducted, and how are results recorded and reported? 3. How are laboratory specimens collected and requested? Are quality control practices systematically implemented in laboratories to ensure Good Laboratory Practice? Data Systems and Electronic Medical Records (EMRs): 1. Are EMRs in use, and how many different systems are there? Are they open-source, and is there interoperability between systems? 2. Are EMRs used only for HIV or for other infectious diseases as well? If so, which ones? 3. Is EMR information completed in real-time, or is data initially collected on paper and later entered? What is the time interval between paper data collection and EMR entry? 4. Have EMRs been evaluated? What were the findings, and were corrective actions taken? Unique Identifiers: 1. Are unique identifiers used for labeling individual records? If not, are there plans to develop health or national unique identifiers? 2. What types of patient or client identifiers (e.g., full names, national ID cards) are used in the country? Are there differences across regions?
